en: The *Compendium of the Unhindered Great Compassionate Heart Great Dharani Sutra*,
which extracts immeasurable meanings from a single dharma;
the directions and the power of the great vows of the various honored ones of the five families in the Southern Potalaka Ocean Assembly who fulfill all aspirations.
At that time, Bhagavān, dwelling in the samādhi of the sovereign power of the Great Dhāraṇī of Unobstructed Compassion,
expounded the characteristics of the Noble Great Maṇḍala.
If one wishes to know the majestic deportment, physical forms,
and ritual requirements of the deities of the five families, as well as the mudrās of these ocean-like deities,
one should first know the names of the fingers: the lotus-joined palms.
The lotus is principle (*tattva*). Since wisdom must reside where there is principle, it is represented by the left and right hands. Their names are "Wisdom" and "Principle.
Because the left hand is quiescent, it is named the "Womb-treasury Ocean of Principle."
The right hand accomplishes all activities; it is named the Wisdom Vajra Ocean.
The five fingers of the left hand are the Matrix Ocean of the Five Wisdoms;
the five fingers of the right hand are the Vajra Ocean of the Five Wisdoms.
The left hand represents concentration (samādhi) and the right hand wisdom (prajñā);
the ten fingers are the ten perfections (pāramitās), or alternatively called the ten dharma-realms, or termed the ten suchnesses (tathatās).
When contracted, they encompass the one; when expanded, they possess distinct names and numbers.
The left little finger is *dāna*; the ring finger is *śīla*;
the middle finger is *kṣānti*; the index finger is *vīrya*;
the thumb is *dhyāna*; and the right little finger is *prajñā*.
The ring finger is the square; the right middle finger is the vow;
the right index finger is power; the right thumb is knowledge;
the left thumb is wisdom; and the left index finger is the square.
The left middle finger is the *praṇidhāna* (vow); the ring finger is the *bala* (power).
The right thumb is the *dāna* (generosity) space-wheel (*ākāśa-cakra*).
The right index finger is the *śīla* (precept) wind-wheel (*vāyu-cakra*). The right middle finger is the *kṣānti* (patience) fire-wheel (*tejas-cakra*).
The ring finger of the right hand is the water wheel; the little finger of the right hand is the dhyāna earth wheel— the little finger is earth, the ring finger is water,
the middle finger is fire, the index finger is wind, and the thumb is space.
These are the names of the ten pāramitās;
it is not that these venerable positions are currently being employed.
That which may now be employed is as follows.
Samādhi, wisdom, and the principle of suchness—
through these, one should understand the mudrās of the various honored ones.
The Five Families of Honored Dharmas: First, for the rite of pacification (*śāntika*), one employs the honored ones of the Buddha Family;
thus there are five wisdom Buddhas. Second, for the rite of increase (*puṣṭika*), one employs the honored ones of the Ratna Family.
Therefore, there is the "Jewel-Radiance-Banner Smile":
for those seeking merit, it is the jewel;
for those seeking wisdom, it is the radiance.
For those seeking official rank, the banner is used;
for those seeking respect and affection, the smile is used. For the rites of subjugation, the deities of the Vajra family and others are employed.
Therefore, there are five great wrathful deities and four deities of the Lotus family for the rites of love and respect.
Therefore, the principal deities such as Avalokiteśvara and others, who employ the five methods of summoning, belong to the Karma-kula.
Consequently, the hook, noose, chain, bell, and so forth enter into the Dharma-body of the five wisdoms.
Therefore, there are five wisdom-vessel noble ones who constitute the self-nature body (*svābhāvikakāya*) of the lotus.
Therefore, there are four kinds of lotuses that constitute the enjoyment body (*saṃbhogakāya*) of the Buddha.
Therefore, there is the emanation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) of the Tathāgatas and others, which is like donning armor.
Therefore, there are thirty-two bodies; because Vairocana Tathāgata is the source of the five Mother-families and the Lord of the Buddha-family, he has no mother.
This is as stated, for example, in the Vairocana Sūtra.
The syllable A is the seed-syllable of Vairocana Buddha;
the syllable HŪṂ is the seed-syllable of Vajrasattva.
(From the *Vajraśekhara Sūtra*).
The syllable HŪṂ is the seed-syllable of Vairocana;
the syllable A is the seed-syllable of Vajrasattva.
This is the ritual procedure for the Vajra Ocean.
Thus, in every assembly,
one should know that these two characters alternate with one another, acting as both principal and attendant to benefit sentient beings.
Even when Amitābha (Puṭa-hai) passes into parinirvāṇa through great compassion, he likewise manifests ten billion bodies.

They act as mutual lords and attendants to guide and transform all sentient beings: Akṣobhya Tathāgata, Lord of the Vajra Family, has Vajrapāramitā as his consort; Ratnasaṃbhava Tathāgata, Lord of the Jewel Family, has Ratnapāramitā as his consort; Amitāyus Tathāgata, Lord of the Lotus Family, has Dharmapāramitā as his consort; and Amoghasiddhi Tathāgata, Lord of the Karma Family, has Karmapāramitā as his consort. This is according to the principle that the four Buddhas are born from the four pāramitās.
The mind possesses the principle that the four Buddhas mutually give birth to the four pāramitās.
In that case, do the four pāramitās constitute the fathers and the four Buddhas constitute the mothers?
He said, "It cannot be obtained.
"Why can it not be obtained?
He replied, "The four pāramitās constitute both concentration and wisdom."
Then the four pāramitās cannot be considered the primary [leaders], but the four Buddhas are the primary [leaders].
It is, for example, as when parents together give birth to children; although both are the progenitors, the father is not designated as the mother.
These are correlated with the five wisdom wrathful deities:
Akṣobhya-vajra is the wrathful form of Vairocana;
Prajñāpāramitā Bodhisattva is the wrathful form of Trailokyavijaya; and Aśvaghosha-vajra is the wrathful form of Akṣobhya Buddha.
The wrathful deities of the Svabhāvacakra: Vajrasattva Bodhisattva, Krodha-Kuṇḍalī, Ratnasaṃbhava Buddha, and the wrathful [deities];
the wrathful deities of the Svabhāvacakra: Vajragarbharāja Bodhisattva, Ṣaḍbhuja (Six-Legged One), Amitāyus Buddha, and the wrathful [deities].
The Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva of the Svabhāvacakra, the Vajrayakṣa, and the wrathful Amoghasiddhi Buddha:
the Svabhāvacakra is itself the body of tranquility.
Furthermore, Vajra Ucchuṣma is the wrathful manifestation of Amoghasiddhi Buddha;
his essential nature is the wheel of vajra activity.
Ucchuṣma is the Bodhisattva Ucchuṣma, who is the wrathful manifestation of the invincible Śākyamuni Buddha.
The deities of the Svabhāva-cakra are Maitreya Bodhisattva, Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara, Amitāyus Buddha, and the Wrathful One.

In the Svabhāva-cakra, Avalokiteśvara is the principal figure, and his consort Tārāvajriṇī is the White-Robed Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. These thirty-seven deities constitute Vairocana Buddha, the All-Illuminating Vajra.

All that follows is the same as the four Buddhas of the four directions described above: In the east is Akṣobhya, the Vajra-pāramitā; In the south is Samantabhadra, the Ratna-pāramitā; In the west is Amitābha, the Dharma-pāramitā; In the north is Amoghasiddhi, the Karma-pāramitā. Sādhu, the Sovereign Tathatā-king of wondrous activity, mastery, love, great joy, and delight; Ratna-maniprabha, Ojaḥ-ketu, Pūrṇa-praṇidhāna, Hasita, Nandana, Dharmaviśuddhi, Śrī-prajñā-hetu, Avaivartika-vāk, Svabhāva-śūnyatā-karman, Kauśalya-rakṣa, and Vīrya; Daṃṣṭra-tīkṣṇa-muṣṭi-guhya; Lāsya-vyākaraṇa-mālā-prema; Gīta-abhaya-nṛtya-ṛddhi; Gandha-apratigha-puṣpa-varṇa; Dīpa-samanta-avabhāsa-vilepana-samanta-viśuddhi; Aṅkuśa-kuśala-udbhava-pāśa-samādhi; Śṛṅkhala-dṛḍha-dhāraṇa-ghaṇṭā-vimukti.
Having thus completed the explanation of the wheel of the wrathful nature of the various deities,
now the first realm is described: within the supreme inner ground of the subtle marks of the principal deity, there is an eight-petaled lotus.
Its wondrous colors are blue and yellow; its wondrous jewel-vajra stem constantly emits immeasurable light.
A hundred thousand kinds of exquisite colors intermingle to adorn the ground, which is made of deep-blue lapis lazuli.
Within a golden realm and a deep blue field, subtle and peerless,
from the heart of this flower pedestal, there appears a great lunar disc.
Within it is the form of the Honored One, known as Thousand Hands and Thousand Eyes.
Sublime form transcending the three realms, golden-hued and replete with radiant brilliance;
his head bears a topknot crowned with a jeweled tiara, from which dark blue hair flows down over the summit.
He possesses five hundred faces and is endowed with a thousand eyes.
Within the jeweled crowns upon his various heads, he abides as the body of a manifested Buddha;
his physical form possesses a hundred arms. Among them, he gathers various jewels;
in his left hands, he holds the sun-essence pearl and the palace-manifesting pearl.
Left: the *khaṭvāṅga* bead; left: the precious bow bead;
left: the *vajra* bead; left: the noose bead;
left: the red lotus bead; left: the white lotus bead.
Left: *Ratnapeṭaka-maṇi* (Jewel Casket Pearl); Left: *Viniyata-maṇi* (Calmness Jade Ring Pearl); Left:
*Viniyata-ratnādarśa-maṇi* (Calmness Jewel Mirror Pearl); Left: *Viniyata-drākṣā-maṇi* (Calmness Grape Pearl); Left:
*Viniyata-buddha-maṇi* (Calmness Buddha-Transforming Pearl); Left: *Viniyata-ratnaśaṅkha-maṇi* (Calmness Jewel Conch Pearl).
Left hand holds a vajra; left hand holds an iron hook and a rosary.
Left hand holds a white whisk and a rosary; left hand holds a precious vase and a rosary.
Left hand holds a wish-fulfilling jewel; the ten lotuses are joined as symbols of concentration and wisdom.
The aforementioned Wisdom Moon-Essence Jewel; the aforementioned Wisdom Color-Cloud Jewel;
the aforementioned Wisdom Cane-Jewel; the aforementioned Wisdom Treasure-Sword Jewel;
the aforementioned Wisdom Treasure-Arrow Jewel; the aforementioned Wisdom Kamaṇḍalu Jewel.
The above is the King’s Jewel of Wisdom; the above is the Purple Lotus Jewel of Knowledge.
The above is the Blue Lotus Jewel of Wisdom; the above is the Precious Sūtra Jewel of Knowledge.
The above is the Golden Wheel Jewel of Wisdom; the above is the Skull Jewel of Knowledge.
The aforementioned Wisdom Willow-Bead; the aforementioned Wisdom Crown-Bead;
the aforementioned Wisdom Jewel-Bowl-Bead; the aforementioned Wisdom Three-Swords-Bead;
the aforementioned Wisdom Battle-Axe-Bead; the aforementioned Wisdom Fearlessness-Bead.
To the right is the Wisdom-Jewel Seal-Bead;
each arm is adorned with exquisite jewels like *nyagrodha* branches, with bracelets and rings as armlets,
hundreds of thousands of precious necklaces, wonderful garlands, and celestial robes.
Adorned with a wondrous body of jewels, the Savior possesses perfect radiance;
free from fever, he dwells in samādhi. Seated in the full-lotus posture with the right leg over the left, he rests upon a sublime jewel lotus; his wondrous marks are peerless.
Having already explained the central image and concluded the discussion on majestic deportment and auspicious signs,
I shall now explain the excellent characteristics of the great bodhisattvas upon the eight petals,
as well as the methods for pacifying, increasing, majestic deportment, and physical form.
Upon an eight-petaled lotus pedestal, beginning from the northeast and circling clockwise, is Avalokiteśvara with the Amoghapāśa [mudrā].
He wears a crown of five topknots upon his head and abides in the form of a transformation Buddha.
He possesses three sets of nine faces and eyes; his central face is white in color.
With a smiling and compassionate countenance, his left and right sides display a dark blue wrathful form subduing Māra;
his body is adorned with exquisite necklaces and a deerskin *kāṣāya*, his form graced by a hundred blessings.
With four arms and two legs, his left hand of samādhi opens a lotus flower, while his other left hand holds a noose; alternatively, he may hold a rosary.
His right hand of prajñā forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma, or he may hold a vajra-chain.

To the right is Prajñādhṛtīśvarī, holding a chain; she dwells upon a thousand-petaled lotus with the light of exquisite lapis lazuli, seated in the full-lotus posture with the right foot pressing upon the left.
Next is Bhṛkuṭī Avalokiteśvara.
Wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, his body is the color of white flesh;
he has one face and two eyes with a joyful and compassionate expression.
He possesses four arms and two legs; in his left hand, he firmly holds a lotus flower.
The left hand of means holds a vajra, and the right hand of wisdom grasps a rosary;
the right hand displays the wish-granting mudrā.
Adorned with a garland of exquisite jewels and blue lotuses, as well as celestial robes, necklaces, and most sublime garments.
Seated upon a thousand-petaled lotus in the full-lotus posture with the right leg pressing upon the left is the Eleven-faced Avalokiteśvara;
his hair is bound in a topknot crown, and within that crown resides the body of a Buddha.
The front face is pale yellow, with an expression of compassionate salvation;

the left and right faces are dark blue-black. The three faces on the left display wrathful expressions, while the three faces on the right display the subduing of Māra; behind them is a face of violent laughter.
The Tathāgata form upon the crown has four arms and two legs;
the left hand in the mudrā of meditative concentration holds a lotus,
while the right hand in the mudrā of wisdom bestows fearlessness— or alternatively, forms the fist-seal.
The aforementioned Jñānadhara holds a rosary; he is adorned with garlands, exquisite necklaces, celestial robes, and upper garments.
Possessing the wondrous color and radiance of a conch shell, he dwells upon a thousand-petaled lotus, seated in the paryaṅka posture with the right foot pressing upon the left.
Next is Hayagrīva Avalokiteśvara.
Upon his head is a precious horse-head with three faces, each possessing three eyes;
in the center of his jeweled crown resides the body of a manifested Buddha.
The physical form is the color of raw flesh, with an exceedingly wrathful expression;
sharp fangs protrude above the lips. He has four arms and two legs, his body forming the mudrās of Samādhi and Prajñā;
the left hand forms the fist of *Dhyānaprabha*.
The wheel of the precepts of *kṣānti* (patience) is bent; the right [hands] extend the wheels of *vīrya* (diligence), *dhyāna* (meditation), and *prajñā* (wisdom) like a beak.
Wisdom is likewise so. The hands of concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom join at the head, resting slightly below the chest;
this is the characteristic of the left fist-seal of concentration (*samādhi*).
The aforementioned Prajñādhara holds a battle-axe; adorned with garlands and exquisite necklaces,
clad in celestial garments and subtle robes, possessing the wondrous color of lapis lazuli light,
he dwells upon a great lotus flower, seated in the paryanka posture with the right foot pressing upon the left.
Next is the wrathful hook Avalokiteśvara.
Upon his head is a crown of flaming hair; he has the form of a four-faced Vidyārāja.
His front face is white-flesh colored, with eyes possessing the appearance of a great man.
The left and right [hands] are green and blue in color; he displays a great wrathful aspect.
The left hand holds a noose (*pāśa*), and the right hand of wisdom grasps an iron hook (*aṅkuśa*).
The right hand of knowledge forms the mudrā of granting boons (*varada-mudrā*). His body is adorned with exquisite necklaces and ornaments.
Wearing garments of celestial garlands, with the radiance of a thousand-colored lotus,
he sits upon a great precious flower in the full-lotus posture with the right leg placed over the left;
next is Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara.
Wearing a subtle and wondrous great jewel crown, with the body of a Buddha abiding upon his head;
his countenance bears an expression of compassion, his body is pale yellow in hue, and he possesses six arms and two legs. With his left hand, he firmly presses Mount Māra.
The left [hand] of the Wisdom-Reasoning (Prajñā) holds a lotus; the left [hand] of the Stability (Samādhi) holds a golden jewel.
The right [hand] of the Wisdom-Reasoning has the gesture of contemplation; the right [hand] of the Wisdom possesses the wish-fulfilling gem.
The right [hand] of the Stability holds a rosary; they are adorned with garlands and exquisite necklaces.
Wearing the celestial robes of a *kāṣāya*, with a halo the color of a lotus flower,
seated upright upon a great lotus, with the left leg raised and the right in the full-lotus posture—
this is Amoghapāśa Avalokiteśvara.
Wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, with three faces and three eyes on each;
the central face is white in color, possessing a wrathful and terrifying expression.
He has four arms and two legs, and in his left hand he holds a hook atop a lotus of meditative concentration.
The left hand of means holds a lasso; the right hand of wisdom holds a vajra-hook.
The right hand of knowledge grasps three swords. He is adorned with garlands, necklaces, and saffron robes as celestial garments, and possesses the subtle radiance of a lotus flower.
Seated upon a great precious lotus in the full-lotus posture with the right leg over the left, there is the single-tufted Rākṣasa Avalokiteśvara.
He wears a crown of flaming hair atop his head; he has one face, which is dark blue-black in color.
With a most great expression of wrath, his four-armed and two-legged body holds three swords in the left hands of Samaya;
the left hand of Naya holds a noose, while the right hand of Prajñā holds a precious sword;
the right hand of Jñāna holds a battle-axe and a sword.
Adorned with garlands and necklaces, wearing the saffron-colored *kaṣāya* robes,
with a halo of a hundred jewel-hues, they sit in the full-lotus posture with the right foot placed over the left.
Having thus described the eight bodhisattvas, their majestic deportment and physical forms are complete.
Now, the second court’s rite for increasing and prolonging life is explained.
The Tathāgata Akṣobhya of the east has a body of reddish-white color, with the appearance of the newly risen morning sun.
The left hand forms the fist-seal of determination; the right hand, representing wisdom, touches the knee.
His body is draped in a saṃghāṭī robe. He dwells peacefully within a moon disc, possessing the pure golden light of Jambudvīpa, seated upon a white elephant throne.
To the south is the Tathāgata Ratnasaṃbhava.

His physical form is golden-yellow in color. With his left hand he forms the fist of meditative concentration, and with his right hand of wisdom he opens the outer square; he bends his ring fingers and little fingers.
In the description, the thumb of the central [figure] is prominent; his body is clad in the *bōrúo* (field-of-merit) robe,
radiating a golden brilliance, seated upon a precious horse—
this is the Tathāgata Amitāyus of the Western Quarter.
The physical form is vermilion-gold in color; he forms the *samādhi-mudrā* with eyes gazing downward.
Clad in robes of vermilion light, he dwells within a great lunar disc, entering meditative absorption to extract suffering from the body.
With the radiance of purple-polished gold, seated upon a peacock throne,
is the Tathāgata Amoghasiddhi of the north;
his body is crimson-gold in appearance, and his left hand forms the fist-mudrā of meditative concentration.
With the right hand, extend the five fingers; place it upon the right side of the chest.
Adorned with the saṃghāṭī robe of a field of merit, one abides within a full moon disc, universally radiant with golden light, seated upon a garuḍa throne.
In the northeast is Bodhisattva Maitreya.
Upon his head is a crown of exquisite jewels; his body is the color of white flesh.
In his left hand, in the gesture of meditative concentration, he holds a purple lotus flower, upon which rests a *kundikā* (water flask).
The right hand rests upon the knee; the body of the Savior of the World is adorned with all manner of exquisite necklaces and ornaments.
Samantabhadra Bodhisattva dwells peacefully within the lunar disc in the southeast of the ocean.
Wearing a crown of exquisite topknots upon his head, his physical form is the color of white flesh, manifesting the aspect of great compassion and pity.

His left hand holds a hook atop a lotus in the mudrā of meditative concentration, while his right hand forms the fist of wisdom resting upon his knee. He is adorned with hundreds of thousands of varieties of necklaces and ornaments.
Adorned with pearl necklaces, celestial garments, and the colors of all exquisite jewels,
her essence is compassion; she sits upon a great precious lotus flower,
its full lotus-rings radiant, resting securely upon a mandala of the full moon.
In the southwest is Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva.
His crown consists of five topknots; his body is golden-yellow in color.
In his left hand he holds a blue lotus flower, upon which are three swords.
To the right, Prajñā holds a Brahma-casket;
her body is adorned with exquisite jewels, and her circular halo is the color of a conch shell. She dwells within a moon disc, facing northwest, as Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Upon his head is a great precious crown, in the center of which appears the form of Amitāyus,
white in color. He wears a lotus flower in full bloom representing the ten perfections,
celestial garments, exquisite saffron robes, and wondrous necklaces of myriad virtues.
Adorned with golden light, his body’s radiance pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*.
Abiding within a moon disc in the lotus posture with the right foot pressing upon the left,
he is next to the eastern gate, where Vajrapāramitā is in the south.
Adorned with a crown of five topknots on his head, his body is the color of a dyed ocean;
in his left hand, held in the mudrā of meditative concentration, he grasps a lotus flower upon which rests a Brahma-casket;
in his right hand, held in the wisdom-mudrā, he forms the seal of Akṣobhya; he is draped in saffron robes and exquisite necklaces.
Adorned within the blue-black [maṇḍala], she dwells within a moon disc at the northern side of the eastern gate.
Tārā Bodhisattvī has a topknot crown upon her head, and her physical form is bluish-white in color.
The appearance of a middle-aged woman: With the perfect, all-pervading radiance of the blue lotus of concentration and wisdom, Her brilliance shines like pure gold;
she smiles, clad in fresh white robes, Adorning her body with boundless splendor.
At the eastern gate of the southern door is the Great Vairocana Tathāgata.
He dwells upon the crown of a celestial tiara adorned with a *vimala* mani-jewel and a hundred precious gems;
at its summit reside five Buddhas, their bodily forms golden in color.
With the seal of meditative concentration and wisdom,
adorned with billions of jewel necklaces, flower garlands, and exquisite celestial robes,
his entire body is arrayed with every kind of jewel and possesses the radiance of a thousand-colored conch; he sits upon a lion throne.
On the western gate is Ratnapāramitā.
She wears a crown with five topknots; her body is the color of white flesh.
In her left hand, held in the gesture of meditative concentration, she holds a lotus flower, upon which is a jewel.
To the right is the four-cornered wheel of wisdom; his body,
adorned with the marks and signs of excellence and graced by a fine saṃghāṭī robe and exquisite necklaces,
dwells within a moon disc at the western gate as the Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Upon his head is a crown of five topknots; within the crown resides the Vidyādhara body, white in color.
His left hand holds a white lotus in the mudrā of meditative concentration, and his right hand displays the mudrā of teaching the Dharma. He is adorned with exquisite garlands and precious necklaces.
Her body is adorned like that of Avalokiteśvara; she dwells within the lunar disc at the northwest gate as the Dharma-pāramitā.
She wears a crown of five topknots, and her physical form is the color of white flesh.
With the seal of entering meditative concentration through samādhi and wisdom, upon a lotus flower,
wearing a Brahma-casket and a fine monastic robe with exquisite necklaces— adorned with the bodies of ten thousand *siddhas*,
his circular halo pervading the Dharma-realm— he dwells peacefully within a lunar disc.
On the east of the northern gate is Karma-pāramitā.
She wears a crown with five topknots; her body is azure-green in color.
Her left hand, held in the mudrā of meditative concentration, grasps a lotus flower, upon which rests a Brahma-casket.
To the right is the Wisdom-Karma-Vajra; adorned with the saṃghāṭī robe and exquisite necklaces, his wondrous jewel-body dwells within a moon disc.
This is the Bodhisattva generated from the Lotus Family at the western lotus of the northern gate.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is the color of white flesh;

he possesses the compassionate aspect that rescues the world. Endowed with the thirty-two major marks, his left hand holds a red lotus in the mudrā of meditative concentration, while his right hand, in the mudrā of wisdom, touches his knee.
His body is adorned with a garland-kāṣāya, jeweled necklaces, celestial robes, and exquisite rings and bracelets;
thus adorned upon his sublime body, he dwells in a great lotus-moon palace. Having thus described the second enclosure,
The arrangement of the deities is complete; now the rites for enrichment and subjugation of the third enclosure are explained.
At the eastern gate is the Life-Extending Avalokiteśvara, wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, within which resides the body of a Buddha.
His physical form is deep yellow in color; with a compassionate and supple countenance, he rescues the world.
With twenty arms, he draws in and receives all classes of living beings;
his two feet bear the mark of the wheel-spoke, as he transforms and guides all sentient beings.
The left *ding* hand holds a precious jewel; the left *li* hand grasps a precious sword.
The left *ding* hand wields a golden wheel; the left *li* hand holds a vajra-kila.
The left *ding* hand carries a shield; the left *li* hand holds a vajra-gong.
The left hand of samādhi holds a vajra-bell; the left hand of principle forms the great lotus mudrā.
The left hand of samādhi holds a rosary; the left hand of principle forms the fist mudrā.
The right hand of wisdom grasps a trident; the right hand of knowledge wields a vajra-sword.
To the right is the Buddha-image of Prajñā; to the right is the Vajra-jewel of Jñāna.
To the right is the jewel-mirror held by Prajñā; to the right is the vajra-noose of Jñāna.
To the right is the bestowing of fearlessness by Prajñā; to the right is the *vajra* of Jñāna.
In his right hand he holds a five-pronged vajra of wisdom;
in his right [hand] he wears hundreds of thousands of kinds of *vidyā*-vajra necklaces.
Adorned with exquisite garlands and celestial robes, his sublime body is encircled by a halo that reaches everywhere.
Abiding upon *pāṭala* flowers, the Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Avalokiteśvara is securely established at the southern gate of the great lunar disc.
Adorned with five hundred various crowns, each [deity] dwells within a Buddha-body.
The body of the Thousand-Eyed, Ten-Armed One is golden-yellow in color.
The right hand of Samādhi holds a blossoming lotus; the right hand of Nīti holds a noose;
the right hand of Prajñā holds a great lotus; and the right hand of Jñāna holds a jewel rosary.
The left hand holds an open lotus; the mudrā of joined palms for concentration and wisdom represents the samādhi of principle and wisdom.
With a thousand dharmas that fulfill all vows, every aspiration is brought to perfection; her great vows are as deep as the ocean.
Extensively delivering all sentient beings, he constantly employs the five powers of wisdom to guide and receive all;
during times of royal peril and the blade of war,
he acts as a King of Blades to save them, and during times of pestilence and calamity.
He acts as a King of Physicians to save them; when they suffer from famine and thirst, he becomes a donor out of compassion for living beings;
when they face fear and urgent distress, he becomes their refuge and support; even unto the tides of the ocean.
He manifests as many kinds of fish and appears in the form of a white dog to benefit those who take refuge; for the sake of benefiting all beings,
he manifests ten trillion precious swords and ten billion exquisite necklaces.
Adorned with celestial robes and jeweled garlands, his sublime body is graced by a radiant halo that pervades the entire Dharma-realm;
seated upon a *padma* flower in the full-lotus posture with the right foot over the left,
he dwells at the western gate— this is Avalokiteśvara, known as Vighuṣṭaśabda.
Upon his head is a great precious crown; that crown rests upon the Buddha’s body, whose physical form is golden in color.
Eighteen arms appear for the sake of reaching out to receive sentient beings;
this is the aspect of Great Compassion that saves the world.
The left hand in the mudrā of transformation holds a Buddha-body; the left hand in the mudrā of principle holds a crystal bead.
The left hand in the mudrā of concentration holds a wish-fulfilling jewel; the left hand in the mudrā of principle grasps a Brahma-casket.
The left hand in the mudrā of concentration embraces a palace; the left hand in the mudrā of principle holds a vajra-noose.
The left hand of Samādhi holds a vajra-bell; the left hand of Prajñā forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
The left hand of Samādhi bestows fearlessness; the right hand of Prajñā holds a vajra.
The right hand of Jñāna holds a crystal jewel; the right hand of Prajñā wields a precious sword.
Right: Wisdom-Vajra Chain; Right: Wisdom-Holding Sharp Spear.
Right: Wisdom-Jewel Rosary; Right: Wisdom-Holding Trident-Extinction.
Right: Wisdom-Dharma-Teaching Mudrā; Right: Wisdom-Also Dharma-Teaching.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of varieties of necklaces and various jewels,
he illuminates the world to bring beings to perfection; seated in the full-lotus posture with the right leg over the left,
he constantly dwells upon a great lotus flower, abiding within a great lunar disc.
At the north gate is the Bodhisattva Acala (Ucchuṣma).
His topknot is encircled by white serpents; his body is of a great blue color, adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces, and he possesses an exceedingly wrathful appearance.
Six-armed and six-legged in body, the left hand of method holds the *tandana* seal;
the left hand of concentration grasps a spear and a mallet. The left hand of method wields a golden wheel;
the right hand of wisdom grasps a precious sword. The right hand of wisdom bears the mark of a battle-axe.
Adorned with immeasurable vajra-jewel necklaces, The left hand holds a jewel rosary;
The right hand of wisdom holds a three-pronged [vajra];
The seal of the right hand’s wisdom fulfilling vows Bends the fingers according to the square of wisdom and the vow.
The Wisdom-Force (Jñānabala) has a face of *tathatā* (suchness);
he wears a garment of animal skin, with two red serpents coiled and draped over his chest, their heads facing the central deity; he likewise has four arms and two shoulders.
A serpent encircles him; his color is intensely blue-white as he dwells upon a lotus in a jewel pond in the northeast.
On the crown of his head is a flaming topknot, with the color of a dark cloud and a flash of lightning.
With six faces and eighteen eyes, his extremely great wrathful aspect blazes with flames surpassing all lightning;
he sits upon a water buffalo in the southeast as Acala.
Upon his topknot are eight lotus petals; a lock of hair from his crown hangs over his right shoulder.
He gazes intently with a single eye, his face marked by water-wave lines, and he is greatly wrathful with bared white fangs.
With his left hand, held in the mudrā of concentration, he grasps a noose.
To the right, Prajñā holds a precious sword; her body is wrathful,
adorned with vajra jewel necklaces and fierce flames, abiding upon a seat of flat rock in the southwest as Trailokyavijaya.
Wearing a crown of skulls and flaming hair, with the color of summer rain clouds,
possessing three faces each with three eyes, laughing "Aṭṭaṭṭa" with a smile,
and endowed with hundreds of thousands of arms grasping various weapons.
Manifesting the form of eight arms, because of fulfilling vows and great aspirations:
The left hands of concentration hold a spear to eliminate [afflictions], The left hands of principle embrace a precious bow,
The left hands of concentration hold a vajra-noose, And the right hands of wisdom hold a vajra-bell.
The right hand holds the jewel-arrow; the right hand grasps the jewel-sword.
This is the Seal of Wisdom and Skillful Means that Saves the World.
First, press the left *samādhi*-wrist over the right *prajñā*-wrist, and with the right thumb-wheel (*aṅguṣṭha-maṇḍala*), [perform the gesture].
The left thumb (śam) rests upon the earth-wheel (pṛthivī-maṇḍala); it is like a suspended lotus.
The left index finger (niścaya) and middle finger (vīrya) rest upon the water-wheel (ap-maṇḍala), while the ring finger (kṣānti) and little finger (tejas) are bent into the palm;
likewise, the thumb (śīla) rests upon the wind-wheel (vāyu-maṇḍala).
The *dāna-śūnya-cakra* (charity-void wheel) is held upright,
each [finger] joined to its neighbor with tips like the two sides of a beak; the right [hand], likewise representing wisdom (*prajñā*),
is adorned with a precious necklace of vajra-jewels as an ornament for the body.
With a body of lightning-like radiance and a wreath of flames pervading everywhere,
The left foot treads upon Mahādeva, and the right foot treads upon the Queen of Heaven;
May their evil minds be liberated, and may they take refuge in the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha.
In the northwest is Mañjuśrī (Muṇḍalī),
with a topknot crown of skulls; he has the appearance of lightning and black clouds,
three eyes, and a terrifying expression, with eight arms wielding various weapons.
The left hand of *dhyāna* holds a *vajra*; the left hand of *nīti* holds a trident.
The left hand of *dhyāna* holds a *vajrāṅkuśa*. The right hand of *prajñā* grasps a double-pronged [vajra];
the right hand of *jñāna* makes the fist and presses against the flank. First, form the *vajramuṣṭi*.
Upright is the wind-wheel of the precepts; beneath the right flank, the right hand of wisdom bestows fearlessness.
This is the Great Wrath Seal of Samādhi and Wisdom:
first, with the wrist of the right hand of wisdom, press upon the top of the left hand of samādhi.
Each forms the vajra-fist; with the wheels of concentration,
wisdom, morality, wind, patience, and great diligence, each is held upright against the chest,
with the thumbs and little fingers forming armlets, and adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces.
Adorned with golden bracelets on his arms and ankles, he wears a garment of the skin of the king of beasts;
his two feet rest upon white lotuses. Twelve serpents encircle him, two hang from his neck, and two coil around his two shoulders.
Eight serpents coil around his eight arms; he possesses a most terrifying appearance.
Sometimes he manifests a thousand arms, known as the Thousand-Armed Amṛta;
or he manifests eight arms, each [holding] the noble Mañjuśrī.
Sometimes he manifests with two arms; as Nyi-ma-padma and Kuṇḍalī, he thus appears in ten thousand forms.
He remains far removed from all calamities within a great blazing fire, his majestic power unfathomable.
The Great Wrathful One, Śākyamuni; the Great Bodhisattva Vajragarbharāja, whose nature is the Wheel;
and Vajrarati, the Bodhisattva of the South, who manifests her form at the eastern gate for the purpose of subduing Māra.
Wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, his body is the color of white flesh;
with his left hand in the mudrā of meditative concentration he holds a precious bow, and with his right hand of wisdom he holds a precious arrow.
He is adorned with a necklace of vajra-jewels, celestial garments, and flower garlands.
Her body is adorned with exquisite jewels; she sits upon a lotus seat with the radiance of a lunar disc.
Next is Vajrarati Bodhisattva, wearing a great jewel crown upon her head, her physical form the color of white flesh.
Forming the fist-mudrā of samādhi and wisdom, place it upon the breast;
adorn the body as if with love. The light of the body completely surrounds the sixteen great bodhisattvas, whose majestic deportment is identical in essence.
To the north of the eastern gate is Vajrarāja Bodhisattva.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of white flesh, and he holds the mudrā of the combined fists of Samādhi and Prajñā. His bodily adornments are as described above.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajrasattva.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his bodily form is the color of white flesh;
his left hand forms the vajra-fist at his waist, and his right hand holds a three-pronged wisdom-vajra.
To the east of the southern gate is Vajraprabha Bodhisattva.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of flesh;
his left hand forms the fist of meditative concentration, while his right holds the lunar essence-gem of wisdom.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajraratna.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of white flesh;
his left hand forms the mudrā of Samādhi and Varada, and his right hand holds the wisdom vajra-jewel.
To the west of the southern gate is the Bodhisattva Vajradhvaja.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his bodily form is the color of white flesh, and he holds the jeweled banners of samādhi and prajñā. His body is adorned as described above.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajrahasa.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of white flesh;
he forms the mudrā of the union of concentration and wisdom with his fists; and his ears are raised and tilted to the side.
To the west is the Bodhisattva Vajratīkṣṇa, with a great jewel crown upon his head; his body is golden-yellow in color;
in his left hand, he holds a casket upon a lotus of meditative concentration, and in his right, a wisdom vajra-sword.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajradharma.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of white flesh, and he holds a lotus flower supported by both concentration and wisdom. His bodily adornments are as described above.
In the northwest is the Bodhisattva Vajrahetu.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his bodily form is the color of white flesh;
his left hand forms the vajra-fist at his waist, and his right hand of wisdom grasps a golden wheel.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajrabhāṣa.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is the color of white flesh;
he possesses the tongues of the Tathāgatas of Samādhi and Prajñā; and his ornaments are as described above.
To the east of the northern gate is Vajradaṃṣṭra Bodhisattva.
He wears a great jewel crown upon his head; his body is white-yellow in color, and he holds the mudrā of samādhi and prajñā at his chest. His bodily adornments are also as described above.
Next is the Bodhisattva Vajramuṣṭi.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is a deep blue color.
With the mudrās of Samādhi and Prajñā as vajra-fists, he raises the seal to his chest.
With arms slightly bent and hanging down, his mind is focused;
he adorns his body as he speaks of the upper northern gate, where the Bodhisattva Vajrapāla resides.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown, and his physical form is azure-blue in color.
Left hand: extend the index finger; the remaining fingers are all bent and raised, resting against the side of the armpit. Right hand: the wisdom hand is likewise.
Next is Vajrakarma Bodhisattva.
Wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, his body is the color of white flesh;
with hands joined in the mudrā of concentration and wisdom, he raises them to rest upon his crown.
Having thus described the third enclosure, the arrangement of the deities' positions is complete.
Now, the method for the rites of attraction and enrichment for the fourth courtyard is explained.
At the eastern gate is Gopaka,
who wears a great jewel crown upon his head and whose bodily form is the color of white flesh.
With the purple lotus of meditative concentration and wisdom, and garments of exquisite jewel necklaces,
he manifests the form of Śakra, Lord of Devas, at the southern gate to guide and receive sentient beings; this is Sudhana the Youth.
The youth with a topknot crown, his body the color of white flesh,
holding a red lotus of concentration and wisdom, possessing the aspect of universal compassion—
this is Mārīcī at the western gate.
The form of the Goddess Śrī: her face is the color of a peach blossom;
she holds a white lotus of concentration and wisdom. Adorned with hundreds of thousands of kinds of necklaces, her body is of exquisite hue; she manifests a celestial form to save the world.
The Buddha’s body at the North Gate is forty-eight spans of purple-golden hue. The Muni, the Sugata, displays the marks of auspiciousness:
his left hand is settled in the gesture of meditative concentration with the knee extended in ease, while his right hand forms the mudrā of preaching the Dharma through wisdom.
With the luster of crystal and conch, the Bodhisattva Vajradīpa resides upon a padma flower in the northeast;
he wears a great jewel crown upon his head, and his physical form is the color of fresh flesh.
Holding a lamp of samādhi and wisdom, his body is adorned as described above.
To the southeast is the Bodhisattva Vajragandhā,
wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, his physical form being a deep blue color.
The vessel for the incense-unguent of meditative concentration and wisdom is as described above for adorning the body.
To the southwest is the Vajragandhā Bodhisattva;
she wears a great jewel crown upon her head, and her physical form is a deep black color.
Holding a censer with concentration and wisdom, her body adorned as described above.
To the northwest is the Bodhisattva Vajrapuṣpa;
she wears a great jewel crown upon her head, and her bodily form is pale yellow in color.
Holding fresh flowers with concentration and wisdom, adorning the body as described above:
Avalokiteśvara at the South Gate wears a leaf-garment.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown, and from his topknot appears Amitāyus.
The physical form is the color of white flesh; the left hand displays the mudrā of preaching while the right, representing wisdom, holds an unopened lotus.
With the luster of a conch and *kuṃuda* flowers, he smiles as he sits upon a white lotus, seated in the full-lotus posture with the right leg pressing down upon the left.
Next is Ghaṇṭāpāṇa-yakṣa.
With the body and head of an elephant king and the form of a human, his body is blue-yellow in color;
his tongue pervades the entire dharma-realm. His left hand is in the mudrā of meditative concentration, pressed against his waist.
To the right is Prajñāvajraghaṇṭā, adorned with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and garments,
possessing a majestic and powerful appearance, with flaming garlands enveloping her entire body;
next is the Ṛṣi Agastya.
Lean and emaciated, with the color of raw flesh, holding a vase upon a lotus and surrounded by a halo of blazing light— this is the White-Body Avalokiteśvara,
dwelling on a lotus petal at the northern side of the eastern gate.
Wearing a great precious crown upon his head, his body is pale yellow in color;

he manifests the aspect of Great Compassion that rescues the world. His left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration and preaching the Dharma, while his right hand, representing wisdom, holds a lotus flower. His body is adorned as previously described.
Next is Khaṇḍakapālin: with the head of a white elephant and a human body, his physical form is a brilliant white;
his left hand forms the mudrā of the meditative fist, while his right hand of wisdom holds a precious sword.
Adorned with bracelets, armlets, necklaces, and garments, and surrounded on all sides by flaming garlands;
next is the seer Asita,
whose physical form is the color of white flesh, holding the treasury of the Dharma-jewels.
With a thin, wrinkled, and naked form, he is surrounded by a universal garland of flames;
Avalokiteśvara is situated above the eastern gate,
wearing a great jewel crown upon his head, with a physical appearance the color of white flesh.
The left hand is fixed in the gesture of preaching the Dharma; the right hand holds a white whisk of wisdom.
Upon the fresh white discs of the sun and moon, he stands upon a *padma* flower, followed by a parasol and a *viṇā*.
With the head of a white elephant and a human body, his form is the color of white jade or snow;
he holds a white parasol and is adorned with rings, bracelets, and exquisite necklaces,
possessing the marks of great majestic power, with blazing flames pervading his entire body.
Next is the sage Virūḍhaka;
his physical form is the color of raw flesh. Holding a sage’s staff with concentration and wisdom, his body radiates a brilliant, blazing luster as he dwells peacefully amidst fierce flames.
On the western side of the southern gate is the Correct Avalokiteśvara.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his physical form is the color of white flesh.
His left hand holds a red lotus of meditative concentration, and his right hand holds a red lotus of wisdom.
The Savior possesses the marks of being beloved and respected; his body is adorned as previously described.
Next, he embraces the hook-bearing Piṇāka-nāga, who has the head of an elephant king and a human body, with a deep crimson complexion.
The left hand is an empty fist resting upon the waist;
the right holds a wisdom-vajra hook and bracelets, adorned with exquisite necklaces.
Possessing the marks of great majestic power, his body is encircled by flashes of lightning, his adornments being immeasurable.
Next is the Seer Gautama;
his physical form is the color of raw flesh. He holds the precious *bhadraghaṭa* vessel and possesses the marks of great supernatural power (*mahābhijñā*), with flames arising all around him.
To the south of the western gate is Avalokiteśvara of Southern Radiance.
Upon his head is a great jewel crown; his body is deep yellow in color, with an expression of subtle joy.
His left hand is in the mudrā of preaching the Dharma.
To the right, he bestows wisdom and fearlessness; with a hundred kinds of exquisite flower garlands, necklaces, and celestial robes, he adorns the body as previously described.
Next follows the flower garland *viṇāyaka*.
With the head of a white elephant and a human body, his physical form is the color of a white crane;
he holds a flower garland with both concentration and wisdom.
Possessing the marks of great power, he is adorned with bracelets, armlets, and exquisite necklaces, while fierce flames envelop his entire body.
Next, one visits the Immortal Kong.
His physical form is the color of white flesh; he holds a great jewel casket and possesses the marks of great supernormal power, surrounded by a pervasive, great blazing flame.
To the north of the western gate is Avalokiteśvara of the White Abode.
His hair is bound in a crown and he wears pure robes; his body is white-yellow in color.
His left hand holds a *padma* (lotus) in the mudrā of meditative concentration, while his right hand forms the mudrā of wisdom with the fist hanging down.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of kinds of necklaces as described above, he next grasps the rope-mantra *pīṭhana-yakṣa*.
His physical form is the color of a red lotus; he has the head of an elephant king and the body of a human.
The mark of his tongue fills the world; his left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration pressed against his waist, while his right holds the wisdom-vajra lasso.
He possesses the marks of great majestic power, with a wreath of flames pervading his entire body, adorned with rings, bracelets, and exquisite necklaces.
Next is the Accomplished Immortal (Siddha).
His physical form is the color of raw flesh; he holds the trident seal and possesses the marks of great majestic power, abiding amidst a wreath of flames.
At the eastern side of the north gate, please behold Avalokiteśvara.
Upon his head is a great jeweled crown; his body is white-yellow in color.
His left hand, in the mudrā of meditative concentration, holds a *kundikā* (water jar); his right hand, in the mudrā of wisdom, bestows fearlessness.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of necklaces as previously described for the body,
he next holds a bow and arrows;
he has the head of a white elephant and a human body, his physical form being the color of snow.
With his left hand of stability he embraces a precious bow, and with his right hand of wisdom he holds a precious arrow;
adorned with exquisite bracelets, rings, and necklaces, his entire body is enveloped in a garland of flames.
Next is the Rishi Vasu.

The Great Sage Avalokiteśvara resides at the western side of the northern gate, within a mass of blazing flames. He possesses the marks of great spiritual efficacy and is seated upon a blue lotus of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Upon his head is a great jeweled crown, and his body is the color of white flesh.
With compassion, he saves the world; his left hand holds a fresh lotus in the gesture of stability, and his right hand, through wisdom, bestows fearlessness.
His body is adorned as previously described, and he next embraces the Lokeśvara-Śṛṅkhalā-Piśāca.
The physical form is dense and majestic; the left hand holds the Vajra-shackle and the right hand grasps a radish.
His majestic power is towering and his appearance brilliant like the radiance of the morning sun, with flaming garlands encircling his entire body.
Next is the seer Atiṛi, whose physical form is stained crimson;
he holds a seer’s staff and manifests the signs of great supernormal power,
with a wreath of flames encircling his entire body.
Having thus completed the description of the positions of the deities in the fourth court,
I shall now explain the method for summoning and donning the armor in the fifth court.
At the eastern gate is the Bodhisattva Vajraghaṇṭā.
Wearing a sublime jewel crown upon his head, his body is a deep blue color;
his left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration with the fist clenched, while his right hand holds a wisdom vajra-bell.
He is adorned with all manner of precious necklaces, celestial garments, and saffron robes.
Adorned with a body of wondrous jewels, with a halo like the colors of a rainbow,
and dwelling amidst *puṇḍarīka* flowers, [is] the Bodhisattva Vajrāṅkuśa at the southern gate within the great full moon disc.
Wearing a wondrous jewel crown upon his head, his bodily form is of a dark, majestic hue;
his left hand forms the mudrā of the clenched fist of meditative concentration, while his right hand holds the wisdom-vajra hook.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of precious necklaces, his body is arrayed as previously described.
To the west is the Bodhisattva Vajrapāśa.
He wears a crown of exquisite jewels upon his head; his body is white-yellow in color.
His left hand holds a vajra-noose at his waist, and his right hand forms the wisdom-fist resting upon his knee.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of kinds of necklaces as previously described for the Vajraśṛṅkhalā Bodhisattva of the Northern Gate,
she wears a sublime jewel crown upon her head, and her bodily form is the color of white flesh.
The left hand forms the fist-seal; the right hand holds the wisdom-vajra-lock and hundreds of thousands of exquisite necklaces.
Adorning the body as previously described, he is the messenger Tārā in the northeast.
Her body is azure-blue in color; she holds a purple lotus of meditative concentration and wisdom.
She has the appearance of a young maiden, adorned with a jeweled crown and exquisite necklaces, surrounded by a blazing wreath of flames, her body as majestic as that of Avalokiteśvara.
The messenger of the Lotus Family in the southeast has a body of white-yellow hue. The central deity has the appearance of a youth;
his samādhi and wisdom are represented by a red lotus, and he is adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces.
A great garland encircles his body; his bodily form is adorned as described above.
To the southwest is the messenger Kuntali, whose bodily appearance is dyed blue and who has the aspect of a wrathful one with bared white fangs.
With the appearance of an elderly man, holding a vajra atop a lotus,
his great hair adorned with jeweled necklaces and a flaming garland adorning his entire precious body—
he is the northwest messenger, Amoghapāśa.
His physical form is the color of white jade and snow;
he has the appearance of a wrathful yakṣa and holds a cintāmaṇi jewel.
Adorned with vajra necklaces, his body is like that of Avalokiteśvara, with a mass of flames pervading his precious form.
At the southern gate of the east is the body of a Brahmin;

his face is the color of raw flesh. He has the appearance of a bhikṣu-monk, wearing white lay garments of plain silk, and holding a *khakkhara* staff [as symbols] of meditative concentration and wisdom.
Next is the body of a mahoraga:

with the head of a serpent and the dignified appearance of a nobleman, he holds a flute or a pipe with his hands of concentration and wisdom, or perhaps tosses a drum; his majestic deportment is like that of the celestial hosts.
Next is the body of a Śrāvaka.
His physical appearance is the color of white flesh;
he has the youthful features of a bhikṣu and holds a triple-layered robe case, his body draped in a saṃghāṭī.
Next is the body of the bhikṣuṇī:
her skin is plump and white in color; she holds a red lotus flower and bears the appearance of an elderly woman; her body is clad in the saṃghāṭī robe.
The body of the Bhikṣu at the Eastern Gate:
his skin is wrinkled and his flesh is the color of raw meat;
he possesses the majestic marks of great virtue, wearing a turban and a kāṣāya robe, holding an alms bowl and sitting upon a grass mat.
Next is the body of the Kinnara King, with the heads of a deer, a gazelle, and a horse;
holding musical instruments, his human body is naked in appearance. Next is the body of Vaiśravaṇa.
Wearing a great precious crown upon his head, his face is deep yellow with a wrathful expression that subdues Māra;
in his left hand he holds a kīla-staff and a jeweled stūpa as symbols of samādhi, while in his right he holds a precious sword as a symbol of prajñā; his body is clad in armor and robes.
Adorned with the precious *kaṣāya* and jeweled necklaces, his body is further graced by celestial robes.
Next is the body of a civil official;
the face is the color of raw flesh, and he displays the mudrā of joined palms representing meditative concentration and wisdom.
His body is clad in ceremonial robes, possessing the appearance of a high-ranking official;
he is a lay follower (upāsaka) from the east of the southern gate.
His face is the color of white flesh, wearing a white crown and a garment of a hundred knots.
Holding the vessel of practice, he has the appearance of a white-robed layperson,
yet his form is not that of a human being;
his body is a great azure color, and in his left hand he firmly holds a drawn bow.
To her right is Prajñādharā, holding a bow and arrow; next is the goddess Kumārī, appearing like a fierce Caṇḍāla.
Her body is the color of white flesh, and she holds a purple lotus representing concentration and wisdom.
Out of compassion for all beings, he manifests the forms of gods and humans,
adorned with exquisite garlands and precious necklaces; his body is most wonderfully sublime,
appearing next as the form of a minor king.
The face is the color of raw flesh; she wears a crown of exquisite jewel garlands;
her hands are joined in the mudrā of combined wisdom and skillful means; her body is clad in deep crimson;
she is the Upāsikā at the southern gate, facing west.

The face is of a pale white flesh-color; she has the appearance of a woman with long hair and half-closed eyes in an expression of loving reverence; she holds a lotus in her wisdom hand, and next [to her] is a nāga body.
The physical form is a great blue color; upon the crown of the head appears the face of a dragon with an expression of wrathful fury.
With the hands of meditative concentration and wisdom, he grasps black clouds, followed by the body of Maheśvara.
Upon his head is a wondrous celestial crown; his face is like a purple lotus.
He embraces a sharp spear with his hands of meditative concentration and wisdom.
He rides upon a great black water buffalo and is adorned with divine robes, flying garments, and exquisite jewel necklaces.
Her body is adorned with subtle and exquisite colors, and she dwells within a moon disc.
Next is the female form;
her face is the color of white flesh, resembling that of a celestial maiden.
The aspect of loving respect and cherishing; a subtle and exquisite color adorning the body.
To the west is the gate of the Southern Heaven-body.
The physical marks are the color of a red lotus; in the left hand, she holds a lotus-flower casket in the mudrā of meditative concentration.
Possessing the wisdom of the wondrous lotus, with a celestial robe and a body of a hundred merits;
next is the form of a yakṣa,
with a crown of flaming fire upon his head and a physical appearance the color of raw flesh.
The eyes are like flashes of lightning; with samādhi and prajñā, he holds the three-pronged [vajra].
Next is the body of a Pratyekabuddha:
his skin is the color of white flesh, with the appearance of a middle-aged bhikṣu.
The ten lotuses of concentration and wisdom are joined; her body is clad in the robes of a field of merit.
Next is the form of a young maiden;
her face is the color of white jade and snow, with the appearance of a woman in her early years.
Holding a blue lotus, he dwells at the northwest gate of the exquisite jewel-flower;
his face is the color of white flesh,
and his physical form possesses the marks of a noble person.
Holding a wondrous lotus flower, his body clad in the saffron robe of merit;
next is the form of a gandharva,
with an eight-cornered crown upon his head and a physical appearance the color of raw flesh.
His body is like that of a great bull-king; his left hand, representing *samādhi*, firmly holds a flute and a transverse flute, while his right hand, representing *prajñā*, wields a precious sword.
He possesses the marks of great majestic power, with a topknot crowned by a wreath of blazing flames, and he next holds a vajra-body.
The physical form is the color of raw flesh; he has the wrathful aspect that subdues Māra.

His hair is tied in a topknot adorned with a crown of flaming garlands. His left hand forms the mudrā of meditative concentration pressed against his waist, while his right holds the wisdom vajra. He is adorned with vajra-jewel necklaces.
Wearing celestial garments and skins of beasts, his body is adorned with the colors of exquisite jewels;
next is the form of a young boy,
with a face the color of white flesh, having the appearance of a tender youth.
Holding a lotus flower with concentration and wisdom, his body is clad in garments of exquisite jewels;
he is the Great General of the Eastern Heaven of the Northern Gate.
His face is the color of raw flesh, and he joins his palms in both concentration and wisdom.
His appearance and deportment are like those of Śakra; his body is adorned with the colors of exquisite jewels.
Next is the body of a garuḍa;
its physical form is dark blue-black, and its face is that of a winged bird.
With a majestic and naked form, his human body is endowed with wings;
his left hand forms the mudrā of concentration at the waist, while his right hand holds a wisdom-vajra hook.
Next is the body of Mahābrahmā.
Wearing a sublime celestial crown upon his head, his face is the color of white flesh;
he has four faces, each with three eyes, and an eight-armed, two-legged body.
His left hands are held in the mudrā of meditative concentration, grasping a trident, while his other left hands hold a lotus.
The left hand of *dhyāna* holds a *kamaṇḍalu*; the left hand of *nīti* holds a white whisk.
The right hand of *prajñā* forms the fist seal; the right hand of *jñāna* holds a sharp spear.
The right hand of *prajñā* holds the mirror of the four wisdoms; the right hand of *jñāna* bestows fearlessness.
His body was adorned with exquisite necklaces, celestial robes, and the kāṣāya;
his sublime form was graced by a halo as he sat upon a white lotus,
positioned next to the elder’s body.
The face is the color of white flesh; he holds a wish-fulfilling jewel (*cintāmaṇi*) and wears the garments of one who is honored.
He possesses the physical marks of a person of great wealth and nobility, and his body is that of Īśvara at the western gate of the north.
The face is of a white-flesh color; he holds a red lotus,
wears a jeweled crown and celestial garments, and is fully endowed with the marks of Śakra,
followed by the form of an asura.
Three faces, blue-black in color; wrathful and naked in appearance;
six arms and two legs in body. With the mudrā of joined palms representing samādhi and wisdom, the left hand holds a crystal fire-stone, and the left [other] hand grasps a sword and staff.
To the right is Prajñāmbu-sphaṭika; to the right is Jñānadhara holding the seal of a balance.
Next is the body of Śakra;
within his jeweled crown on the crown of his head, he wears a vajra-club.
The face is of a white-flesh color; the left hand, representing Samatha, forms the fist-mudrā, while the right hand, representing Prajñā, holds a single-pronged vajra.
Adorned with hundreds of thousands of varieties of necklaces, celestial garments, and flying robes, they are arrayed in robes of wondrous jewels.
Within a lunar disc of radiant light, he dwells upon a sublime lion throne;
next is the body of a layman,
with a face of white-flesh color, holding a maṇi jewel.
Wearing formal ceremonial robes, with the appearance of a great householder or elder—
these thirty-three [deities] abide with their bodies upon the petals of a great lotus within a moon disc.
Having thus explained the five families of honored ones, as well as their positions and physical forms, [the description is complete].
Now, the four kinds of lotuses are described, surrounding the shape and color of the ground:
In the east is the blue lotus; In the west is the white lotus;
In the north is the purple lotus; And in the northeast of the lotus-ground.
Within each of the intermediate directions, such as the southwest, there is a precious vase of wondrous color beyond compare;
upon a seat of flaming garlands and lotuses, the vase contains a great lotus. Next, the four lotus grounds are described.
The lotus gates in the four directions are of a brilliant crimson color,
constantly emitting immeasurable light; next,
from the deep azure-blue [gate] to the space between the second enclosure, the ground is made of gold.
There is a vajra-shape; next, between the second and third enclosures, the ground is made of white silver and has a three-pronged vajra-shape; next, from the third enclosure...
Reaching the space between the fourth enclosure,
the ground is made of gold and has the shape of a single-pronged mallet. Next,
from the fourth enclosure to the fifth enclosure, the ground is made of white silver.
There is the form of Vajra; next, between the fifth and sixth enclosures, the ground is made of gold and has the shape of a five-pronged vajra;
next is the color of the ground of the inner enclosure.
The ground of the second court is light black, scattered with golden flowers;
the ground of the third court is light purple, scattered with golden flowers;
the ground of the fourth court is [light blue].
A deep purple ground scattered with silver; the ground of the fifth court is light blue scattered with golden flowers;
the sixth lotus-ground is deep crimson, the color of *bimba* fruit. This is the ocean of the maṇḍala.
Hanging from it, red flows from the black; therein dwell the various deities within a great lunar disc.
The deities of the *ḍākinī* ocean-assembly abide there, manifesting their abbreviated postures, forms, and colors.
